name: Atomoxetine Hydrochloride
meta: Selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (non-stimulant ADHD medication)
sections: Selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (non-stimulant ADHD medication)
White granular powder (hydrochloride), highly soluble in water.

Originally investigated as an antidepressant (tomoxetine) but found insufficiently effective; later developed and approved as the first non-stimulant for ADHD. First approval/introduction: US FDA 2002 (Eli Lilly and Company).

Selectively inhibits the presynaptic norepinephrine transporter, increasing norepinephrine and dopamine in the prefrontal cortex, improving attention and impulse control without stimulant abuse potential. Receptor / target profile: Selective NET inhibitor (Ki 5 nM), increasing norepinephrine and dopamine in the prefrontal cortex; weak NMDA antagonism.
Hepatic – aromatic ring hydroxylation (CYP2D6), N-demethylation (CYP2C19), glucuronidation
Summary: Bioavailability 63% (extensive CYP2D6 metabolisers) to 94% (poor metabolisers). Tmax 1–2 h. ~98% protein bound. Half-life ~5 h (up to 24 h in poor metabolisers).
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children ≥6 years, adolescents and adults
Children/adolescents ≤70 kg: start 0.5 mg/kg/day; increase after ≥3 days to target 1.2 mg/kg/day (single morning dose or two divided doses); max 1.4 mg/kg/day or 100 mg
Children >70 kg and adults: start 40 mg/day; increase after ≥3 days to 80 mg/day; max 100 mg/day
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Approved from 6 years; monitor growth, heart rate, BP and suicidality.
Use with or within 14 days of MAO inhibitors
Suicidal ideation in children and adolescents – monitor closely
Rare severe liver injury – stop if jaundice
Raised heart rate and blood pressure
Decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
Sudden death in structural cardiac abnormalities
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) – slower titration
Heart rate and BP before and during treatment; height and weight in children; LFTs if jaundice; suicidality.
Somnolence, agitation, GI symptoms, tachycardia, hypertension, rarely seizures. Supportive care.
Michelson et al., Pediatrics 2001 – dose-dependent efficacy in childhood ADHD.
Cortese et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2018 – network meta-analysis: atomoxetine effective, though less so than stimulants.
Capsule/tablet should not be opened (eye irritant)
Report yellow skin, dark urine, mood changes
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
